title: Cow’s milk sales at record low in Britain as people opt for plant-based options
summary:
Environmental and animal welfare concerns, and taste preferences, are behind rising popularity of vegan alternatives

Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with…

blocks.text: Has milk gotta lotta bottle? It may not have as much as it used to, with official data showing Britons are buying less cow’s milk than at any point since records began.

Guardian analysis of the government’s family food survey shows the average person bought 1.8 pints (1,024ml) of cow’s milk a week in 2024-25 – the lowest level in the record’s 52-year history and less than half the amount of milk bought in 1974.

So why are people buying less? One reason, say experts, is that the growing accessibility of plant-based milks has created a mindset shift when it comes to dairy – with even meat-eaters changing their habits.

“You can get plant-based milk in a lot of different places now and the taste isn’t that different,” says Rosie Green, a professor of environment, food and health at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. “People might be worried about animal welfare as well – and then the environmental problems are the icing on the cake.”

Mass produced dairy has a huge impact on the climate. From their digestion and manure, cows emit methane, a gas the government has called a “super pollutant” because it is more potent than carbon dioxide and plays a big role in global heating. The agriculture sector represents 48% of the UK’s methane emissions, with 78% of those produced by cattle.

“But the thing people pay less attention to is [dairy’s] land use footprint, because dairy cows require a lot of land for grazing,” says Ruth Westcott, the director of campaigns at Foodrise. They also require feed, some of which is grown on UK cropland and some imported. Westcott says the shift towards larger, more intensive dairy farms has increased reliance on imported feed.

Experts say animal welfare is another reason why people are turning off cow’s milk as consumers learn more about standard practices in the dairy industry, such as the early removal of calves from their mothers. “People are becoming more aware of what happens on dairy farming,” Sean Barrs, a senior campaigner at Animal Justice Project, says. “They’re seeing more images on the internet of what it looks like and they’re becoming more educated.”

As tastes for cow’s milk have declined, purchases of plant-based alternatives have grown, from an average 37ml to 94ml a week since 2014. The food trends expert Morgaine Gaye says plant milks are no long seen as a “vegan choice” but “an everybody choice”.

“There’s lots of people who eat meat, are not even vegetarian, but have a non-dairy milk in their coffee, have an oat milk on their cereal, just for the taste, because they’ve been exposed to it so much,” she says.

High street shops have played their part in that exposure. The Canteen on Stokes Croft in Bristol stopped selling meat dishes in 2020. This year, they began offering oat to customers before cow’s when serving hot drinks. “We word it like: ‘Do you want oat milk or dairy?’ That really changed habits,” says Liam Stocks, the general manager. “A lot of customers will go: ‘Oh, I will have oats.’ You’re making them feel like it’s the default.”

Stocks says the decline in purchases of cow’s milk speaks to a broader attitude change. “It’s an easy win, right? If you are wanting to be more environmentally friendly, it’s very hard to stop eating meat. I always see [cutting dairy] as a first thing people might do to try and change their behaviour.”

With searing temperatures and collapsing climate talks at the forefront of the discussion, it can be easy to forget how transforming food systems is also imperative to tackling the climate crisis. “Changing your diet is the one thing that most people can do that will have the biggest impact on the environment,” says Westcott. “The climate impacts of our diets have stayed stubbornly high and barely reduced at all since 1990. We’re just not seeing anywhere near the changes that we need.”

The decline in liquid-milk purchases has not meant less milk is being produced. UK production reached a record in 2025, with more milk going into cheese, yoghurt, butter and powders as demand for some of those products grew, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB).
In its latest carbon budget, the government for the first time targeted a reduction in dairy consumption, aiming for a 20% cut by 2035.

Producing less dairy would be a huge step towards sustaining our food systems. Westcott says: “Reducing dairy consumption would free up land in the UK for nature recovery or for growing more food directly for human consumption, like more lentils, peas, beans – more high-protein foods that would allow us to be more food resilient and have a higher domestic food production and need to import less.”

For Green, swapping milk is an easy way to make that difference. “We can’t reach our environmental targets no matter how much we do in transport or energy generation – we have to change the food system as well,” she says. “We need to still eat less meat as well – but switching the milk is a good start.”

Dairy UK, the industry body, says its Dairy Roadmap, run with AHDB and the NFU, has cut the greenhouse gas emissions associated with milk production by 24% since 2008. “The dairy sector plays a significant role in the UK,” according to their website. “Our processing members play a vital role inemploying 22,500 people at processing sites around the country. On top of that, dairy farms employ 50,000 more people, both directly and in supporting industries.
“British consumers show their love for dairy every day. If any evidence were needed to prove that, the fact that 96% of adults buy milk should be proof enough.”
